title: Off-Boarding — Organisational Employee Exit Process Flow
subtitle: BCEA ss.20, 31–42 · LRA ss.186–197, 198–198B · Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (GN 3470, GG 53294) · Income Tax Act Second and Fourth Schedules · Pension Funds Act ss.37A–37D · UIA and UICA · Insolvency Act s.38 · EEA and EE Regulations 2025 · POPIA · As at 19 October 2026

overview.summary: This flow tells an organisation what to do, by when, and who hands off to whom, from the moment an exit is triggered until the last dispute window has closed and the exit data has fed the EE plan and retention measures. It is the closing bookend of the GBS employment lifecycle suite: the Resourcing flow brings a person in; this flow takes them out. It runs one core spine for every exit, whatever the reason, and splits only where the law splits — at the legal gate in Phase 1, which fixes the true legal reason for the exit and therefore the notice, pay and procedure that follow.

notes.text: It does not repeat the procedures that lead to a dismissal. Where an exit is a dismissal for misconduct, incapacity or operational requirements, the GBS Misconduct, Incapacity and Operational Requirements flows govern the decision; this flow starts when that decision is made (and checks, at the gate, that it was made properly) and governs everything afterwards. The flow assumes no collective agreement, bargaining council agreement or sectoral determination regulates exits; where one does and gives the employee more, it prevails.

notes.heading: Legal status
notes.text: The Code of Good Practice: Dismissal (GN 3470, GG 53294) took effect on 4 September 2025, replacing the Schedule 8 Code and the 1999 Code on operational requirements dismissals; it treats incompatibility, imprisonment and expired work permits as forms of incapacity, assesses probation against "suitability for employment", allows small businesses more flexibility, and contains a standard s.189(3) notice in Annexure A. The Code is guidance: decision-makers must take it into account (LRA ss.188(2), 203(3)), but case law applying it is still thin. The legacy uFiling employee-claims portal closed on 20 May 2026 and employees now claim unemployment benefits on UIF Online; the employer portal (declarations and contributions) was expected to migrate to UIF Online by August 2026; as at 19 October 2026 no confirmation that the migration is complete was found, so payroll must confirm the current portal before each declaration. A search on 19 October 2026 confirmed these positions and found no amendment to the Code; re-check before adoption.

notes.heading: Figures in force today
notes.text: BCEA earnings threshold: R269,600.90 a year from 1 May 2026. National minimum wage: R30.23 an hour from 1 March 2026. UIF earnings ceiling: R17,712 a month (R212,544 a year) since 1 June 2021 (GG 44641), so the maximum monthly employee contribution is R177.12; no later increase had been gazetted as at 19 October 2026. Retirement and severance lump-sum table: first R550,000 tax-free, then 18% to R770,000, 27% to R1,155,000 and 36% above. Withdrawal table: first R27,500 tax-free. Both apply to lifetime totals; SARS has confirmed no change for the 2027 tax year.

notes.heading: Labels used throughout
points: LAW = a statute or regulation in force (BCEA, LRA, EEA, UIA, UICA, COIDA, Income Tax Act, Tax Administration Act, Pension Funds Act, Medical Schemes Act, Insolvency Act, Companies Act, Immigration Act, OHS Act, MHSA, POPIA); binding now.

Code = the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025, or the Code of Good Practice on the Prevention and Elimination of Harassment in the Workplace, 2022. Must be taken into account; departures must be justified.
CL = a principle from case law, cited by name, court and year. Verify the citation and any later authority before using it in advice.
DRAFT = a Bill or proposal not yet in force: the Protected Disclosures Bill, 2026 and the two-pot proposals on retrenchment access. Build readiness; do not treat as a current legal duty.
BP = best practice or internal control; not a statutory deadline. Adopt as policy so it becomes binding internally.

notes.heading: Timing conventions
notes.text: N is the date notice is given or received (or the trigger date, for exits without notice). T is the termination date, the employee's last day of employment. Internal periods are working days unless stated. Statutory periods (7 days for final pay, 30 and 90 days for referrals, 6 months under EEA s.10) are calendar days under the Interpretation Act 33 of 1957 s.4, excluding the first day and including the last unless it is a Sunday or public holiday. Periods under the CCMA Rules, 2023 (rule 3) are also calendar days, but a last day falling on a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday moves to the next working day, and the old 16 December–7 January exclusion no longer applies. The 30-day dismissal referral period runs from the dismissal or, if later, from the employer's final decision to dismiss or uphold the dismissal on internal appeal (LRA s.191(1)(b)(i)). Diarise referral deadlines conservatively. Never mix the two in a letter.

notes.heading: Design principle
notes.text: Most CCMA losses on exits come from mislabelling the exit, not from mistakes in the paperwork that follows: a "resignation" that was really a constructive dismissal; a "retirement" with no agreed or normal retirement age; a "contract expiry" where the employee reasonably expected renewal; "abscondment" with no ultimatum. The flow therefore puts a mandatory legal gate at the front, holds every termination letter until the gate is signed, and runs everything after it on one checklist so that pay, documents, access and records are the same whatever the reason.

notes.heading: Eight interpretation points that shape the flow
points: The reason decides everything. These are not dismissals: resignation; retirement at the agreed or normal age; expiry of a fixed-term contract with no reasonable expectation of renewal; death; and termination under Insolvency Act s.38. These are dismissals, each needing substantive and procedural fairness under the Code: misconduct; incapacity; operational requirements; non-confirmation after probation; constructive dismissal (LRA s.186(1)(e)); non-renewal where renewal was reasonably expected (s.186(1)(b)); and "retirement" that falls outside s.187(2)(b). A transfer of a going concern under s.197 is not an exit at all: contracts move to the new employer automatically.

Resignation is unilateral. Once communicated, a resignation takes effect without the employer's acceptance, and can be withdrawn only with the employer's consent. In Toyota SA Motors v CCMA [2015] ZACC 40 the majority (Nkabinde J) refused leave to appeal on review-delay grounds and declined to decide the resignation point; Zondo J's dissenting (minority) judgment analysed resignation and would have held that reinstatement was not competent because the employee was serving notice. Treat that dissenting reasoning as persuasive only, not binding, and check other resignation authorities (for example Mohlaka v Minister of Finance, LC) against current reporters before quoting them.

The constructive-dismissal screen is the employer's best defence. The employee must prove that the employer made continued employment objectively intolerable and that resigning was a last resort (CL: Pretoria Society for the Care of the Retarded v Loots, LAC 1997; Strategic Liquor Services v Mvumbi, CC 2009). A documented offer of the grievance route, made before the resignation takes effect, is the strongest answer.

Retirement is only safe at a proven age. Dismissal on account of age is fair only where the employee has reached the normal or agreed retirement age (s.187(2)(b)). The agreed age comes from the contract; the normal age from practice or fund rules (CL: Rubin Sportswear v SACCAWU, LAC 2004). An open-ended stay-on made a later retirement automatically unfair in Datt v Gunnebo Industries (LC 2009). Schweitzer v Waco (LC 1998) supports retiring an employee at any time after the age, but a contrary view (that protection applies only at the age itself) has been expressed; act promptly, or record a stay-on with a fixed end date.

Pay first, argue later. Final pay is due within seven days of termination (BCEA s.32(3)). A deduction is lawful only with written consent to a specified debt, or where the law allows it; loss or damage deductions also need fault, a fair procedure, an amount no higher than the loss and a cap of one quarter of the employee's remuneration in money (s.34). Employer claims are pursued through s.34, civil action or a Pension Funds Act s.37D request, never by self-help set-off.

Two-pot has changed fund exits. From 1 September 2024 one-third of contributions go to the savings component and two-thirds to the retirement component. The retirement component is preserved until retirement; resigning or being retrenched does not unlock it. Vested rights from before 1 September 2024 keep the old rules. Proposals to allow retrenchment access are DRAFT only, and fund rules on the vested component differ.

Death benefits do not follow the will. Under Pension Funds Act s.37C, trustees have up to 12 months to trace and allocate the benefit among dependants and nominees. In Mutsila v Municipal Gratuity Fund (CCT 228/23) [2025] ZACC 17 the Constitutional Court held unanimously that dependency is assessed as at the date of the member's death, rejecting the SCA approach in Fundsatwork v Guarnieri (SCA 2019). Never promise a nominee a benefit.

Exit data is now a compliance input. The 2026 EE reporting cycle (1 September 2026 to 15 January 2027, online) is the first in which employers are measured against annual targets aligned to the sectoral numerical targets. Terminations by designated group feed EEA2, and exit reasons feed the EEA12 barrier analysis. An employer that learns of harassment in an exit interview and does nothing risks EEA s.60 liability, even though the employee is leaving.

notes.heading: Roles used
notes.text: HR Off-Boarding Owner (HRO, the process owner and spine; in smaller organisations the HR manager); Line Manager (LM); Legal / IR (LA); Payroll (PAY); Finance (FIN); IT (IT); Security (SEC); Facilities (FAC); Benefits administrator (BEN); Occupational Health and Safety practitioner (OHP); EE Manager (EEM); Company Secretary (COSEC); Communications (COM); Exit Interviewer (EXI: neutral HR, not the HR business partner who handled the exit, or a third party); HR Analytics (HRA); Senior Sign-off (SSO); EXCO and the EE Committee (EXCO, EEF). The employee (EMP) and their representative (REP); for a death, the executor and next of kin (EXE). External: retirement fund and administrator (FUND); medical scheme (MS); group-risk insurer (INS); SARS; UIF; Compensation Fund; trustee or liquidator (TRU); TES; CCMA or bargaining council; Labour Court (LC).

stages.title: Phase 0 — Readiness (standing obligations)
intro: Phase 0 has no case trigger. It must be in place before the first exit, because most off-boarding failures are fixed before the notice arrives: there is no asset register to recover against, no written consent for the loan deduction, no agreed retirement age in the contract, no restraint worth enforcing.

notes.heading: Employee side of Phase 0
notes.text: Nothing is owed yet, but the employee's later position depends on this phase. An employee who never signed a specific loan-deduction consent cannot have the loan deducted from final pay, whatever they owe; and an employee whose contract names no retirement age cannot safely be retired without proof of a normal age.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: The single most common Phase 0 gap is the missing asset register. Without it, Phase 4 becomes an argument, and an argument is where unlawful set-offs start.

stages.group: Phase 1 — Exit trigger, verification and legal gate
stages.title: Phase 1 — Exit trigger, verification and legal gate
intro: Phase 1 establishes the true legal reason for the exit, chooses the branch, and holds the termination until a legal check confirms it. N is the day the trigger reaches any manager, not the day HR opens the file.

notes.heading: Employee obligations at this stage
notes.text: Resign in writing (except an illiterate employee); state the notice being given; raise any grievance before resigning if the reason is the employer's conduct; tell the employer promptly of any change of mind, knowing withdrawal needs consent.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: LM → HRO (same day). HRO → LA (gate, screens). HRO → PAY (freeze, expected T). HRO → EEM (designated-group flag). HRO → BEN (death, retirement). HRO → Misconduct, Incapacity or Operational Requirements flow (hold).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Accepting a resignation tendered to avoid discipline and then continuing the hearing is risky once the resignation has taken effect: take LA advice before T, and consider whether the enquiry can conclude during the notice period.

steps.title: Log the trigger and open the file
steps.trigger: Resignation letter; disciplinary, incapacity or s.189 outcome; retirement date; contract end date; notice of a death; liquidation or sequestration order; TES end-of-assignment notice; permit expiry.
steps.action: Record: trigger type; date received; how received; employee status flags (probation, fixed-term, TES, foreign national, union representative, COIDA claimant, discloser, designated group). Open the exit file and the workflow that triggers Phases 2–5.

steps.title: Insolvency

intro: Rights the organisation must not obstruct. Final pay within 7 days; no deductions outside s.34; a certificate of service, with no reason stated unless requested; the UIF declaration and documents needed to claim; information on fund, medical scheme and group-risk options; no annual leave imposed during notice; a truthful and minimal reference; confidentiality of exit-interview data; access and correction of personal information under POPIA; freedom from victimisation for referring a dispute; referral to the CCMA, a bargaining council or the Labour Court.

rows: Loss or damage deductions capped at "one quarter of net pay" / "25% of net pay"
BCEA s.34(2)(d) caps total deductions at one quarter of the employee's "remuneration in money". Use the statutory wording; treat any net-pay reading as a conservative policy choice, not the law.
"Annual leave may not be taken during notice (s20)"
The prohibition is that the employer may not require or permit leave during notice (BCEA s.20(5)(b)), so it applies even at the employee's request. Pay accrued leave out under s.40.
Disputes about s.34 deductions go to the Labour Court, not the CCMA (O'Reilly v CCMA, JR 2395/19)

Not followed: the citation could not be verified. Employees below the threshold may claim unlawfully deducted or withheld amounts at the CCMA under BCEA s.73A (CCMA awards on s.34 deductions are reported); labour inspectors can issue compliance orders; above the threshold, use the courts.

Resolved (19 October 2026): s.73A sets no fixed referral period and the LRA s.191 periods do not apply; refer within a reasonable time, and the Prescription Act s.11(d) three-year period applies to the debt. Do not tell employees one year.
Certificate of service: "In J2525/07 (2009) the Labour Court doubted its s77(3) jurisdiction"
The case is not identified by name. Rely on s.42 and the labour inspector's compliance-order route; verify before citing.
Two descriptions of Gallup's 45% finding: no leader "proactively discussed how their job was going" and a leader "had done little to discuss"
Use one wording: 45% said no manager or leader proactively discussed their satisfaction, performance or future in the three months before they left.
Exit interview held "once final pay is settled" and "before the last day"
Final pay falls due up to T+7, after the interview window. Read as "once final pay amounts are confirmed" (step 5.3).
Consent needed before collecting special personal information in exit interviews

Correct for information volunteered in the interview (health and similar). Race processed for EE purposes already has a lawful basis (POPIA ss.27(1)(b), 29, verify), so EE coding does not depend on consent.
Garden leave: "full pay and benefits, no duties, no access"
Add: a contractual basis or the employee's consent; compensation for average commission where earnings depend on work; and a decision on whether garden leave counts towards any restraint period.
Insolvency is the only financial-distress branch

Add business rescue: under Companies Act s.136 employment contracts continue on the same terms during rescue, and any retrenchment must follow LRA ss.189 and 189A. Do not apply Insolvency Act s.38 to a company in rescue.
Severance-benefit criteria stated without the fall-back
State that a lump sum that does not meet the "severance benefit" criteria is taxed as ordinary remuneration at marginal rates, not on the severance table.
Employee contribution 1% plus employer contribution 1%, subject to the earnings ceiling.
Label as BP: no statute sets the period.
"The employee-claims function of the legacy uFiling system closed in May 2026"
Confirmed: closed on 20 May 2026. Employer services were to migrate by August 2026; confirm current status before telling payroll which portal to use.
Full citation: Truworths Ltd v Nxasana, Mr Price Group Ltd and Another [2025] ZAWCHC 580. The court also enforced a six-month, competitor-limited restraint as proportionate.
Paraphrase in client material and verify the exact wording against the reported judgment before quoting.
s.37D: "since 1 September 2024, a compensation order under s300 of the Criminal Procedure Act counts as a judgment"
Verified (19 October 2026): inserted by the Pension Funds Amendment Act 31 of 2024 with effect from 1 September 2024; not retrospective. Practice is still settling.

intro: BCEA s.32(3) requires final pay within seven days of termination, but SARS directive turnaround is outside the employer's control and the Act has no mechanism for a directive delay. Employers are left choosing between late payment and paying without a directive.
BCEA s.42 creates the duty to issue a certificate of service but no direct sanction; enforcement relies on the general inspection and compliance-order machinery.
Neither the BCEA nor the LRA defines "resignation" or regulates its withdrawal. The rules come from case law, and the only Constitutional Court analysis is in a dissenting judgment (Toyota, Zondo J).
LRA s.187(2)(b) does not define "normal or agreed retirement age" or say when the employer must act, which has produced the Schweitzer and Datt lines of authority.
BCEA s.34(2)(d) refers to one quarter of "remuneration in money" without saying whether that is gross or net of statutory deductions.
The EEA2 termination categories, the UIF termination reason codes and typical HRIS reason codes do not align, so the same exit can be reported three different ways.
POPIA sets no specific retention periods for HR records, so employers must reconcile BCEA s.31 (3 years), TAA s.29 (5 years), EEA s.26 and prescription periods themselves.

The UIF migration from uFiling to UIF Online has proceeded by departmental statement rather than gazetted transitional rules, leaving employers without a formal reference for which portal is authoritative for declarations.
The two-pot legislation does not unlock the retirement component on retrenchment; proposals to change this are not law, and fund rules on the vested component vary.
